maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS

speakeroldname: Hon. lohn C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I undertook some time ago to make a statement to the House concerning the government's reaction to the remaining recommendations of the last instalment of the Le Dain report on treatment. I am
pleased to indicate to the House the action taken to date by the government relative to the report on treatment.
As hon. members are aware, this report was submitted to the government only a few weeks ago. We have already taken significant steps to implement major recommendations contained in the commission's report. These may be summarized as follows: First, with regard to methadone maintenance, recognizing the necessity to rationalize treatment of opiate dependence I announced in the House on February 24, 1972, government action to control the drug methadone used in treatment of heroin dependent persons. I am pleased to announce that my officials are completing arrangements for the designation of physicians who will be authorized to use methadone.
Those so authorized will be considered to possess the necessary expertise and will have available to them necessary facilities and ancillary services to properly utilize methadone. Principles to be used in determining the criteria for good medical practice in the use of this drug are in full agreement with recommendations in this area by the commission.
Hon. members will be pleased to learn that full support for the government's action to control methadone use is being received from the medical profession. The methadone control program I announced on February 24 is expected to be fully operational by June 1, 1972.
Second, heroin maintenance. Included among the recommendations in the commission's report was one which dealt with maintenance of heroin addicts by providing them with heroin. The commission concluded that heroin should be made available for administration by physicians to heroin dependent persons, under very strictly controlled conditions. As I have indicated on several occasions, I felt it advisable to withhold comment on this recommendation pending careful study of it. This study now has been completed and I wish to indicate the government's views on the commission's recommendation.
In arriving at a position on the recommendation I have, of course, been aware of the views expressed by Canadian physicians regarding a heroin maintenance program. As some hon. members may be aware, the Canadian Medical Association has stated it disagrees "in the strongest possible terms" with any program of providing heroin to those dependent on the drug.
Having carefully considered all the factors involved, I have concluded that if patients must be maintained on an opiate drug, use of methadone is to be preferred, on both medical and social grounds, to use of heroin. Furthermore, the possibility of abuse of a heroin maintenance program is intrinsically high, even if one considers the safeguards suggested by the commission. For these reasons the government cannot accept the recommendation

March 29, 1972
Treatment of Drug Addicts
of the commission of inquiry relating to heroin maintenance. We agree with the Canadian Medical Association that there is no place for such a method of treatment in the Canadian setting.
Third, treatment of rehabilitation facilities. Officials of my department have been actively engaged in discussions with their counterparts associated with treatment and rehabilitation facilities for opiate dependent persons. These discussions have centred on the need to establish criteria for the evaluation of treatment programs and the necessity of periodic reappraisal of their effectiveness.
Fourth, use of amphetamines. I announced in the House on February 24 plans to limit the use of amphetamines to the treatment of two relatively rare medical disorders. Physicians wishing to use amphetamines for these two conditions will be required to receive authorization from me for this purpose. Amphetamines will not be permitted for use in the treatment of obesity as with so-called diet pills. Details of the administration of this program are now being worked out in conjunction with the medical profession. Plans are under way to convene an expert advisory group to consider the feasibility of developing an effective amphetamine antagonist and consideration is being given to sponsorship of research in this area.
Fifth, treatment manual. The treatment manual presented in the commission's report is being enlarged and brought up to date through the co-operation of medical consultants. The revised manual will be sent to all physicians in Canada within the next few months.
Sixth, therapeutic communities. Recognizing the general validity of the commission's recommendations regarding the value of therapeutic communities, my department has provided funds to assist a therapeutic community in British Columbia and is completing final details relative to the provision of financial assistance to a second therapeutic community in the Montreal area. Research and evaluation of the effectiveness of these communities are integral parts of the programs.
Seventh, the treatment of alcoholism. My department agrees that alcohol is the most widespread drug dependence problem. Consultations are being held with provincial governments and key provincial agencies to determine what form of assistance the federal government might most appropriately provide in the fields of prevention, education, treatment and rehabilitation of alcohol dependent persons.
May I say in closing, Mr. Speaker, that the commission has identified a number of community treatment service needs for drug and drug related problems. My department had already responded to some of these needs- information for parents and teachers and the development of laboratory services are good examples-and will continue to promote fulfilment of these needs through its non medical use of drugs programs.

maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). This is the quickest action I have ever seen from this government. It was just yesterday that I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) about the drug heroin about which the minister has spoken. If we can get this type of reaction every day, let's keep it up.

The minister spoke of the rationalization of the methadone treatment and the appointment of doctors who are skilled in the art of treating this particular type of addict, and has seen fit to reject the report of his own commission, one which was in keeping with the report of the research committee of the American bar association which only a couple of weeks ago stated that after a full survey it had reached the conclusion that federal centres should be set up across the United States for the treatment of heroin addiction. This is very similar to the recommendation of the minister's commission which proposed allowing physicians to treat heroin addicts across Canada under strict conditions.
However, the Canadian Medical Association after looking at the situation felt, I believe rightly, that there are two sides to this coin, one being the art of interference with the medical profession and their conscience and the other being the power of government to do as they like. You have those two sides of the coin to keep in mind. However, as I say, the CMA after looking at the situation did back the idea the minister has expressed and felt it was safer to treat heroin addiction through the use of methadone in properly oriented centres. The reasoning behind this is obvious. Research facilities are necessary if one is to know how a heroin addict is progressing during his methadone treatment and whether or not the result has been successful. It has to be accepted that this is scientifically necessary in connection with the treatment which addicts ought to take.
The minister went on to speak of the use of treatment and rehabilitation centres. I am not quite clear what he meant in this regard. I am sure the medical profession has not heard of this. I do not believe the minister has consulted the CMA, any other medically oriented body of which I am aware, or the provinces. If he has, we would like to know about it.
This brings me to another point. The minister has often made excuses for not taking action on the ground that he cannot interfere with health and welfare arrangements or seek to control the medical profession because these are areas within provincial jurisdiction. But in this case he takes another position entirely, as far as I can see. He also states that amphetamines have a limited use in the treatment of two relatively rare disorders and that physicians using amphetamines for the treatment of these disorders will be required to obtain authorization. I am sure the minister intended to add "on the advice of medical commissions or medical experts in their particular fields."
The minister said that amphetamines would not be used in diet pills, and we approve of that. However, amphetamines and like drugs are used for other purposes, and used medically correctly. I hope that the minister is not regarding this as a criterion for stepping in and interfering with proper medical practice in this or any other field. On occasion he has stubbed his toe. I need only remind him of the interference that took place in the use of diet on diabetic sweeteners for sugar not so long ago. I am sure he recalls that.
However, I do want to congratulate him for something. It has taken me a long time to get the minister around to
March 29, 1972

realizing and to expressing in the House the fact that alcohol is the most widespread drug dependent problem in Canada and costs us more than the rest of the addictions put together. I congratulate the minister for finally realizing that. I knew that if I kept after him long enough, some day he would get up in this House and agree with me. For that I am very grateful.

maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS
speechtext: We may also be making a start on educating young people of the age to consume alcohol, of the dangers thereof. I sincerely congratulate the minister for taking this step. I also appreciate the fact that he is setting up centres for this purpose. On the whole, Mr. Speaker, I agree with many of the points made by the minister but I ask him to keep in mind that this must not be considered any criterion for interfering with good medical practice or the conscience of the doctor. As the minister said in his statement, this matter falls under the provinces and the medical profession and it is they who must exercise the necessary discipline.

maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second declaration or statement by the minister to the House during the past month or five weeks which we have had to chew, ingest and digest. Fortunately, we have not yet become addicted to the same sort of approach that is advocated by the minister in his statement. With one exception, I look upon the minister's statement as a sort of expanded progress report on the statement that he made on February 24.
With regard to the use of methadone for the maintenance of addicts, the minister has gone a little further in his statement than he went earlier. He said that they are now in the process of selecting those members of the medical profession who will be considered to possess the necessary expertise and they will be authorized to use the necessary facilities and ancillary services that will be made available to them properly to utilize methadone.
However, I suggest that this is a rather vague and ambiguous statement. What is the necessary expertise that a doctor must have? What are the criteria which are to be established? Again, where will methadone be administered? I take it from the February 24 statement that it will be administered in conjunction with the clinics. If that carries with it the implication that these clinics will be in urban areas only, then to the extent that methadone maintenance may have some value, the people living in rural areas and small communities will be precluded from taking advantage of the program.
I suggest that the whole of the medical profession must be involved in the methadone maintenance treatment program so that addicts who want to cease using heroin and move on to the methadone maintenance program will be able to avail themselves of it no matter where they live in Canada. To confine the program to metropolitan areas where there are clinics at the moment would, I think, do a disservice to any value that methadone maintenance may have.
The minister stated that the medical profession is in full support of the government's program to control methadone and the like. I am not overly impressed with the
Treatment of Drug Addicts
opinion of the medical profession as to what methadone is or can be. I do not know of any doctor who uses methadone and I wonder how doctors can know what it is all about. I do know, as I am sure other hon. members do, from conversations with former heroin addicts who have given it up and moved on to the use of methadone that they contend that methadone, its after effects and addiction are worse than heroin itself. I understand that the idea is still endorsed by the state that a person can take intravenously or orally a chemical in order to create for him an internal condition that permits him to escape from reality. This is still the promotion of an addiction type program.
I foresee that when there is a shortage of heroin, heroin addicts will be moving in to see these doctors, who will be chosen for having the necessary expertise, and simply using the methadone program as a substitute for heroin addiction during the time there is a shortage of heroin. As soon as the supply picks up they will go back to the use of heroin. The idea behind methadone maintenance carries with it relatively little in the field of rehabilitation or the moving away from addiction to drugs, because methadone is a drug and the state is saying, "We endorse the concept that you as an individual should continue an existence which is dependent upon a drug, and we classify methadone as a drug that is legal." But this does not touch the core of the problem at all.
The valuable part of the minister's statement-I congratulate him for it, but say he should have done this the day the Le Dain report was made public; he did not have to wait for an opinion on it-was his reference to the fact that heroin should be used and given a semi-legal status to support or maintain an addict where the individual may not desire to follow the methadone treatment, for whatever value that may have for the individual. The minister will recall that on February 24 I made this suggestion to him, and I am glad he has accepted my advice so quickly.
The minister also talks in the statement about therapeutic communities, as did the Le Dain commission, in respect of treatment. The Le Dain commission expressed some very commendable thoughts about therapeutic communities as mentioned both in its treatment report and its first or interim report in which was mentioned, with some commendation, the X-Kalay Foundation program which has been in existence in Vancouver for some time and which now has expanded and moved into Winnipeg. I am pleased that the department, the minister and the government have understood this and are providing some financial support and assistance to the only therapeutic community in British Columbia, as well as doing something about establishing one in Montreal.
I think the minister would be well advised to extend this area of activity of his department and financially support therapeutic communities far beyond the program he has announced. Such communities could be of value to addicts wherever there is need, such as in Vancouver, Montreal, Toronto and other large centres. Having accepted the value of the X-Kalay Foundation, I am convinced that without further examination or study the government should very quickly extend its support.

March 29, 1972
Treatment of Drug Addicts
In respect of the social question, the statement moves away from the need to make a major assessment as to why people, especially younger people, are social dropouts, why there is cynicism among the younger generation, why they reject the values which have been established and built up over the years and why they turn away from the realities of life and substitute the intake of a chemical, no matter of what sort, in order to create for them some kind of subculture within which they feel comfortable.
I think something must be done to establish a different form of society. We should try to create a concept in society that will be acceptable to people so they will not want to take alcohol, heroin, methadone or any other drug in order to live in an unreal situation. The statement misses completely the fact that there are 10, 11 and 12-year old children in this nation and in North America generally who are addicted to heroin and who reached that state by the route suggested by their peers through the intake of chemicals. The statement also misses the point completely that 6, 7 and 8-year old children are able to go to a hobby shop, purchase glue, get high and damage themselves mentally and internally.
In the past few years there has been a fantastic increase in drug abuse. There has been a fantastic increase in the number of people using alcohol, methadone, marijuana, acid and all the other chemicals and psychotropic drugs. The statement of the minister does not do much to cope with this problem and unless something more positive and worth while is done we will have a steady increase in the use of drugs and a year from now we will be in an even worse position.

maintopic: LE DAIN REPORT-STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT ACTION ON RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING TREATMENT OF ADDICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Canadian people will be happy to learn about the decision just announced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) in which the government took into account the recommendations of several Canadian doctors who, upon publication of the Le Dain report, expressed their views on the dangers of drug abuse both under medical control and clandestine.
Mr. Speaker, drug abuse has caused considerable ravages in Canada to date. A commission of ten doctors reported, after the publication of the first volume of the Le Dain report, that in British Columbia alone, 10,000 adults use heroin illegally and that the use of LSD is increasing considerably among the young especially. In addition, marijuana and hashish continue to attract ever more young Canadians.
The House is now studying a program against the illegal use of drugs, with the co-operation of the medical corps. But, to my mind, we have waited too long before taking efficient steps against the use of drugs.
Only a few years ago, sale or distribution of heroin, opium and drugs of all kinds were limited to adults. However, the pushers discovered, in universities, CEGEP's and even secondary schools, a potential clientele lured by the kicks to be derived from the use of drugs.
We therefore witnessed the development of what I shall call a shocking trade with young people in our schools.

And there have been instances, particularly recently, of both Canadian and American police seizing enormous quantities of drugs of all kinds. Nevertheless, distribution continues even at school levels.
Therefore, to be consistent in this fight against drug abuse, a major publicity campaign should be launched first of all, geared more particularly to young people, to make them aware of the deleterious effects of drugs. There should be a concurrent fight against the drug-distributing mafia, which seems to be very well organized.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I am also gratified to see that the minister's release includes a very small paragraph about alcoholism. There again, Mr. Speaker, government coffers are being filled year after year by taxes derived from sales of spirits, but so far very little action is being taken and very little money spent for an anti-alcoholism campaign in Canada. In recent years, the provinces have launched such an offensive, which so far the federal government has not participated in.
I therefore urge the minister to consider the problem and to have his officials, the physicians employed by his department, also study it and give it all the attention it warrants. I think this will benefit all Canadians.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement with respect to dairy policy for the year starting April 1, 1972. The Canadian Dairy Commission has been authorized to implement a program for the coming year that will permit a substantial increase in the base support level for manufacturing milk.
While prices paid to producers for milk are a matter of provincial jurisdiction, the program will provide for an increase in the support price of the order of approximately 20 cents or more per hundred pounds of milk. The Canadian Dairy Commission has been authorized to pay a subsidy on manufacturing milk and cream under its quota system at the same rate as in the year just ending; that is, $1.25 per hundred pounds of milk testing 3.5 per cent butterfat, or 35.71 cents per pound butterfat. The price at which the commission offers to purchase skim milk powder in support of the market price will be 29 cents per pound, up 3 cents from the present level of 26 cents.
There will be no change for the present in the commission's purchase price of butter, which is 68 cents per pound, or of cheddar cheese which is 54 cents per pound. The market price of cheddar cheese has been well above that support level since last July. Emphasis in the program on skim milk powder will provide a better balance between butter and cheese production and should avoid the possibility of the overproduction of cheese.
There is a holdback from payments to producers to finance the cost of disposing of surplus dairy products, mainly skim milk powder, exported at prices below Canadian support levels. While the Canadian support
March 29, 1972

price for powder is being raised by 3 cents a pound, the holdback on each milk shipper's deliveries within his quota will be retained at the 1971 level of 10 cents per hundred pounds of milk. This is possible because of the greatly improved export price. There will be no holdback on cream deliveries within quotas. While the threshold at which over-quota holdbacks apply will revert to the quota level, production patterns will be closely watched and, should production so warrant, exemption levels can be reinstituted retroactively. I refer to the 10 per cent quota threshold.
The program for the coming year, plus the steps taken in the year just ending, and the quota arrangements provide a price to producers which should ensure adequate supplies without risk of serious butterfat surpluses.
The commission's support prices for skim milk powder and cheddar cheese were increased in February, 1971. There was a further upward adjustment in those prices last August, as well as in the butter price. As a result, a downward trend in production was arrested in the last quarter of 1971 and production is now on an upturn. The arrangements for the coming year should consolidate that trend and ensure adequate supplies for Canadian consumers.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to express our thanks and appreciation to the minister for having provided us with a copy of his announcement on our entry into the House. I should like to say that this announcement is not unexpected; as a matter of fact, it is a policy that for many months has been vigorously pressed for by the entire dairy industry. This policy cannot be attributed solely to the political expediency of an approaching general election but is, rather, an act of desperation.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext: It is an indication of another attempt by the government to use the taxpayers' dollars to buy themselves out of a misinterpretation and lack of proper assessment of a major Canadian problem. It is an outright admission by this government that the policy which they have instituted for the Canadian dairy industry during their term of office has been tragically wrong, in its thrust and in its ramifications, for the industry.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext:
As a result of that policy hundreds of thousands of small cream producers have been put out of business, many of the best herds in Canada have been dispersed completely and small cheese factories have been closed down never to reopen. Now the government expects that through the payment of more money at this time they will reinstate the dairy industry of Canada.
The government's policy has resulted in consumers having to pay more for butter and cheese than ever before in the history of this country. It has resulted, for the first time in Canadian history, in producers of agricultural products actually being fined for production. We have seen chaos in the industry. The government was warned

of this by all opposition parties in the House and by the entire dairy industry of Canada. They deliberately introduced a policy of cutbacks in Canadian production at a time when every international food gathering in the world was forecasting a drop in dairy and protein production, saying that it would be necessary for dairy production to be increased rather than decreased.
The final sentence in the minister's statement reads:
The arrangements for the coming year should consolidate that trend and ensure adequate supplies for Canadian consumers.
This is not a statement made in face of the facts but is, rather, a prayer on behalf of the government. To that prayer I say amen.

speechtext: You need some cheering.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN BASE SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext:
It would have been better had the cheering come from the minister. The objectives mentioned in the statement are laudable enough. The government hopes to achieve in this year a balance between supply and demand, to correct the errors made last year when we had a shortfall and to increase payments by a small amount.
I should like to take this opportunity to point out to the minister that certain areas of this policy are in need of adjustment and correction. This dairy policy is probably the beginning of a first major supply management program in a major food area of this country. It is an attempt to achieve a balance between production and consumption. In the process, a great deal of injustice has been done to some small producers in this country and I point out to the minister that these injustices have not yet been corrected. It should be a major concern of the government to correct these injustices, especially in western Canada where cream producers have been denied quotas which they cannot get back. The least the minister could do is correct these injustices.
I know that some producers are getting their payments back, but many are being left out and are being told to buy another herd or to buy another quota. It is a large enough problem for farmers, particularly small farmers, in this day and age to meet the capital costs of machinery and land, without having imposed upon them another capital cost which will be a burden on their farming operations. The minister's department should look at the situation of producers who have continued to produce cream with a minimum return and should now be given a quota. Those who were held down to a low quota should be given an additional quota.
I say to the minister, also, that if we are to have supply management for food, attention should be paid to people who have such a low level of income that they cannot readily purchase adequate supplies of protein which is available in skim milk powder and dairy products. The government should be working on a program to make protein available to the disadvantaged people in our community, and by that I mean the total community of

Canada. I hope that one day he will stand in the House and announce such a policy.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has anticipated our desires today. I had intended to ask him whether the new 1972-73 dairy policy would soon be announced. I thank the minister for having sent us a copy of his statement at the beginning of the sitting.
We are pleased to note that the dairy industry is now popular in Canada. Once, we used to refer somewhat diffidently to the dairy industry in the House, because it was considered as a secondary industry operated by uninteresting, deficient or uneducated people.
I now realize that all Canadians, including hon. members, are concerned with that vital industry whose annual production is worth $2 billion. Indeed, the industry supports to a large extent the rural areas which are more seriously affected by losses of income or unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, there is more still. This industry helps provide some 300,000 jobs, most of them outside the farm. So, this industry concerns all Canadians because not only on farms but outside as well in villages and even in cities there are people who depend on that industry.
I would also say that the subsidies received by industrial milk and cream producers or others in the dairy industry do not benefit only this category of producers. In fact, these subsidies also help the consumer because otherwise he would be required to pay these amounts granted by the government to support higher prices for producers, which would mean a still much bigger increase in prices.
Mr. Speaker, this is no gift by the government to the producers of industrial milk. It is one way to distribute in the fairest possible manner, the purchasing power across the country in order to create an exchange in production between consumers and producers.
In Canada, the proportional value of subsidies equals only 6 per cent of the gross value of finished products, whereas U.S. subsidies for milk products are much higher. Canada is not a leader in this field. Sometimes I hate to see that the moment the government loosens the purse for industrial milk producers we are left with the impression that they are granted important gifts.
The government is convinced of the proper use of these piecemeal amounts which are doled out to industrial milk producers. Fortunately, they are made good use of and we know how to administer them. That is why the situation can be improved and why I suggest to the government and the hon. Minister of Agriculture to do more because this is a good investment which will bring benefits and which will be profitable to the entire population.
However, I am somewhat puzzled by the minister's statement because although there is the matter of an increase of 20 cents or more per cwt. for the year 1972-73, the estimates for dairy products indicate a decrease of $21 million. In that case, will it cost less because production will be down from last year or will the consumer be asked

to make up most of the increase announced by the minister?
In any case, I think it is the government's duty to make the dairy industry prosperous because if it is we can expect that agriculture as a whole will be healthier.
I notice that in its brief the Canadian Federation of Milk Producers made this recommendation, and I quote:
A careful analysis led us to conclude that there was need to adjust the support levels. Our delegates recommended a 50-cent-per-hundredweight increase in the support prices for manufacturing milk because such an increase is imperative if we are to make sure that there is enough milk in stock to meet the demand on domestic markets. Or else, from another standpoint, those increases are necessary to strike a reasonable balance of income relative to the other sectors of society and in order that the new system of supply management be fair and viable.
In my opinion, that recommendation is most sensible. I for one find it reasonable, but an increase of 50 per cent would certainly not have been exaggerated.
In closing, I would like to point out that the minister has already stated in the House that his department is prepared to allocate many millions of dollars to assist small family farms so that they may survive. I find that amazing; having drilled holes in the boat of small enterprises and of small farmers who are about to sink because water is seeping from everywhere, they tell them: Here is a bit of plastic, try to patch up the holes so that you may come safely into port.
In my opinion, the best plastic that they could be given would be a guarantee for more reasonable prices, more in line with the increase in production cost; they would thus be able to get a better income, to have a more waterproof boat to allow them to reach their goal.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SHORT-TERM DISCOUNTING OF PAYMENTS TO INDIVIDUALS BY GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to include under the provisions of the Small Loans Act the practice of the short-term discounting of payments by governments to individuals, such as unemployment insurance benefits, pension payments and income tax rebates, by defining the discount fee charged by persons lending money on this basis as being interest and therefore restricting interest rates charged by discounters to 2 per cent per month. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Canada has signed fishing treaties with Britain, France, Portugal, and Denmark. speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH DENMARK ON CONTROL OF SALMON FISHING ON HIGH SEAS
speechtext: The agreements I tabled in the House yesterday related, of course, to the phasing out of fishing operations within the fishing zones of Canada. That was their purpose. The negotiations with respect to fishing on the high seas are being carried on for a different purpose; these are not Canadian waters we are talking about. We are trying to get Denmark to co-operate in conserving a fish species which is particularly valuable to Canada. These negotiations are continuing. Regrettably, we have not been able to make as much progress with the Danes as we would like. Nor has anyone else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I find it necessary to bring to your attention, Sir, some methods by which the government brings in bills, one in particular. My point of order relates to Bill C-183. It concerns a breach of a custom of the House with respect to the form in which a bill that amends a statute should be presented. On Monday, if I recall correctly, Your Honour was pleased to give a ruling which opened with the following words:
Last week, a number of bills were proposed for introduction to the House. The Chair expressed reservations about certain procedural aspects of those bills. While three were then accepted for introduction after serious consideration, seven were held in abeyance. On Friday last, hon. members were given an opportunity to express views on a point of order which queried whether these bills might not affect the financial initiative of the Crown. A number of members participated in the interesting procedural debate and I have now had time to study their arguments-
Your ruling, Mr. Speaker, then exhaustively analysed the acceptability of these bills. In the result, three were found wanting and four were accepted, but only by giving them the benefit of the doubt. The four acceptable bills were then introduced. Immediately thereafter the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) moved for leave to introduce an act to amend the Canada Labour Code, now Bill C-183.
I do not propose to speak about the distinction in treatment accorded the ten bills presented for introduction by private members and the bill presented for introduction by the Minister of Labour. In the Latin maxim which we use in law, res ipsa loquitur, "the matter speaks for itself."
I make the point that the government has not demonstrated that it possesses any greater skill than private members in preparing bills which are in accordance with the rules. I should like to point out that when the bill was tabled it did not have the recommendation of the Governor General. However, the day after, when the bill was
Canada Labour Code
distributed to our offices the recommendation of the Governor General was included.
Your Honour will recall the warning you issued to the government in the last session with respect to bills. You will also recall the procedural errors that accompanied the tax reform bill. Had the opposition insisted on adherence to the Standing Orders, Your Honour suggested that you might have to shut down the House for weeks while you checked the bill against the budget resolutions. You will also recall, Sir, that only by special order agreed to by the House was it possible to amend the bill. It is not, therefore, expertise that justifies special treatment for the government on the introduction of bills.
I therefore draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that Bill C-183 contains no explanatory note although it proposes to amend a statute. There is no Standing Order that requires an explanatory note in such a case, but almost 50 years of custom have made the practice mandatory. That practice has been swept aside. The Chair, in yesterday's ruling on the bill of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), referred to previous rulings on the substance of explanatory notes. You are probably better aware of the origin of explanatory notes than I am, Mr. Speaker. They are founded in the report of the committee on procedure which was adopted by the House on June 14, 1923. The report recommended that in the following session the House adopt these rules:
1.	In the preparation of bills amending existing enactments the amendments shall not ordinarily be made by clauses which add or leave out words or substitute words for others, but by clauses which re-enect the section, subsection or other minor division, as it is amended.
2.	In the text of the bill, on the left hand page, new matter shall be indicated by such typographical means as may best suit the varying circumstances of each case, such as brackets, italics, underlining, asterisks, etc. Opposite each clause, on the right hand page, the enactment amended thereby, or so much thereof as is essential, shall be printed with the proposed changes to be made therein similarly indicated.
3.	When a clause repeals an existing section, subsection or other minor division of a section, that section, subsection or division, or so much thereof as is essential, shall be printed opposite the clause.
4.	A memorandum by the draftsman explaining briefly the reasons for each clause, shall be appended to the bill, or distributed therewith. Whenever practicable the memorandum shall be printed on the right hand page of the bill, in paragraphs opposite the clauses referred to and numbered correspondingly.
5.	The above rules shall also as far as practicable apply to the reprinting of bills.
Although the House adopted these recommendations, it did not implement them in a subsequent session by incorporating them in the Standing Orders. The other place did make these recommendations rules of that chamber and they are now incorporated in rule 54 of that body. However, as rulings of this chamber bear out, over the past 50 years these recommendations have been applied to bills which propose to amend statutes.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-183 proposes to amend an existing enactment. It does not comply with recommendations 2, 3 and 4 to which I have just directed my remarks; it does not indicate new matter, it does not reprint repealed clauses, nor does it contain any memoranda explaining

Canada Labour Code
the reasons for each clause. What the bill does contain in lieu of these requirements is a preamble. That preamble has one thing in common with the explanatory note of the bill of the hon. member for Skeena: it is lyrical, to some extent it is poetical, but it is not an explanatory note.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) must make his preamble conform more with existing practice and the form that is usual for explanatory notes. I submit that the bill must be withdrawn and reintroduced with proper explanatory notes or, alternatively, that it continue at pro forma first reading stage and with unanimous consent be reprinted with explanatory notes. The bill was introduced only a couple of days ago and a measure as important as this should not be permitted to proceed to second reading stage unless it contains explanatory notes to aid all members of the House.
Mr. Speaker, in order to substantiate my argument I would refer to a bill which was given first reading on February 21, 1972. I refer to Bill C-6. Clause 2 of that bill reads as follows:
The Criminal Code is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 178 thereof, the following part-
It then gets into part IV of the bill. The important point that I bring to Your Honour's attention is that there is an explanatory note, in some detail, on the right-hand side of that bill. This fact strengthens my argument. With the bill in question, Bill C-183 which is a bill to amend the Canada Labour Code, particularly part V, industrial relations, there is no explanatory note whatsoever. I think this omission is fatal to the legal presentation of this bill. I need not remind Your Honour that if I am correct in my conclusions and my point of order, the bill is imperfect.
Lastly, I should like to direct Your Honour to Standing Order 69 which reads:
No bill may be introduced either in blank or in an imperfect shape.
Even though this bill has been introduced I think we are now faced with the problem of an imperfect bill and I would recommend to Your Honour that either of the two alternatives I have pointed out must be adopted.

In fact, it has been brought to my attention that from time to time bills are submitted to the House without explanatory notes being in them. I have two such bills in my hand. Bill C-4 does not appear to have an explanatory note, neither does Bill C-170, an act to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children. It seems that the bill before us does not contain an explanatory note. There is, therefore, nothing mysterious about this particular bill.

My intervention the other day in respect of private bills was to say that when there was an explanatory note, it should not be argumentative but should be in the form of an explanation. I fully agree with the hon. member that it is extremely helpful to the House and hon. members to have an explanatory note for their benefit and to assist in their understanding of legislation. However, the Chair, taking into account the Standing Orders and the long established practice of the House, cannot agree with the contention that the bill before us cannot proceed on the basis of the argument advanced by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to initiate second reading debate on this bill, an act to amend the Canada Labour Code, I want at once to acknowledge the contribution made to the legislation by my predecessor, the Hon. Bryce Mackasey. I know that hon. members will understand when I say that my colleague sincerely wishes he could be with us today when the principles of this bill are being discussed in the House for the first time.
Hon. members will recall that a bill to amend the Canada Labour Code was first introduced on June 28, 1971. At that time my predecessor made it clear that the bill was being introduced at the end of June for the purpose of stimulating public discussion. The bill did not proceed to second reading and lapsed when the previous session of this House terminated. In the intervening eight months my predecessor and I and senior departmental
March 29, 1972

officials have received representations from and consulted with most groups in the country representing management and labour. In addition, we have consulted with provincial ministers of labour. On the whole, the original bill was well received. A few provisions, particularly those relating to technological change and picketing, stimulated much public discussion and comment. The present bill incorporates a number of the suggestions received in response to the government's request for comments.
The bill before the House now proposes amendments to improve the legal framework governing the relationships between organized labour and management in enterprises within federal jurisdiction and also affirms the proper role of government as representative of the public interest in those relationships.
The present act forms part V of the Canada Labour Code and was formerly entitled the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. That act was passed in 1948 and has remained unaltered. It is no small commendation to the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, minister of labour in 1948, and to the drafters of the IRDI Act that it is still functional today. One forgets that at that time we were still in the era of the DC-3 airplane, television broadcasting was still in the experimental stage and the St. Lawrence Seaway had not been built.
Our economic performance in the world is of vital importance to all Canadians and it will increasingly be so as the world's economic environment drastically changes through the rest of this decade and, indeed, the rest of this century. Good industrial relations will play a vital part in our economic performance and, accordingly, they will be the concern not only of the parties immediately involved but of all the Canadian public. It is with these thoughts in mind, Mr. Speaker, that we have approached the amendments to part V of the Canada Labour Code.
The government's objectives in its labour relations policy are to promote social justice and economic development. This will be done by providing the legal framework that encourages the development of an efficient and equitable system for industrial relations based on the cornerstone of collective bargaining. These principles are reflected in a new preamble. The preamble recognizes the long tradition in Canada of labour legislation and policy designed to promote the common well-being through encouraging free collective bargaining and the constructive settlement of disputes.
An essential ingredient of free collective bargaining is freedom of association and protection of the right to organize. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to inform the House that Canada has ratified International Labour Organization Convention No. 87 which was deposited with the ILO on March 23 by the Canadian ambassador, George Ignatieff. Reference to this convention dealing with the right to organize and to be represented by the union of one's choice is made in the preamble to the bill before us today.
Let me now turn, Mr. Speaker, to some of the provisions of the new bill which I believe are consistent with the over-all goal of labour legislation which I indicated earlier. First I would like to deal with the extension of bar-
Canada Labour Code
gaining rights. The bill would extend bargaining rights to professional employees who until now have not been entitled to bargain collectively. We believe that these people have tended in recent years to be put into a kind of no man's land between management on the one side and the organized worker on the other, without the right to be certified. We propose to rectify this. But in doing so we recognize that professional employees have specialized knowledge and training and that they may choose to have their own bargaining unit.
The bill clarifies in a statutory way the present practice of the Canada Labour Relations Board to grant bargaining rights to employees who have supervisory duties over other employees. If, however, such an employee exercises managerial responsibility or is employed in a confidential capacity in matters relating to industrial relations, then he would be excluded from the bargaining unit as he is at present.
The legislation recognizes that share-of-the-catch fishermen and owner-operator truckers are often in a position of such economic dependency that their relationship is more analogous to that of an employee than to an independent contractor. Accordingly, bargaining rights will be extended to such persons in those industries. I must say, in fairness, that there may be some jurisdictional difficulties with respect to the share-of-the-catch fishermen and we believe that this matter should be settled by the courts.
In extending bargaining rights to persons not previously covered we were cognizant of the fact that these groups could indeed organize and at times strike, but at the same time that they were beyond the dispute settlement procedures of the code. This clearly was not a satisfactory situation and militated heavily in favour of the extension of bargaining rights. It is proposed to permit a union which seeks bargaining rights for a unit that has no bargaining agent to apply to the Canada Labour Relations Board for a representation vote if it can demonstrate membership support of at least 35 per cent in the unit.
A union seeking to displace an existing bargaining agent would still be required to claim majority support at the time of the application for certification. The requirements for the representation vote have been eased to provide that the majority would be determined by a majority of the employees actually voting. Previously, the majority was calculated on the number of employees actually in the bargaining unit whether such employees voted or not. This change reflects common electoral practice.
In addition, we have included provisions designed to put bargaining rights acquired by voluntary recognition, and those acquired by certification, on an equal basis. These provisions also offer protection against the abuse of rights granted voluntarily so that a union carrying such rights would be subject to challenge for a one-year period on the ground that it lacks majority support.
The bill also contains provisions designed to carry over bargaining rights when unions merge or when a business or undertaking is sold. In the same vein, provisions are included in the bill which carry over bargaining rights when an agency of the federal government is transferred

March 29, 1972
Canada Labour Code
from the public service to a Crown corporation covered by this bill.
The bill would strengthen and extend the provisions regarding unfair practices in such a way as to offer additional protection for employers and trade unions and for individual employees and trade union members.
The jurisdiction over unfair practices is to be transferred from the courts to the Canada Labour Relations Board because we take the view that these questions are primarily ones involving industrial relations and are not properly dealt with as matters of quasi-criminal law. We think that these questions should be dealt with in a different atmosphere. The Canada Labour Relations Board would be empowered to seek accommodation between the parties through the assistance of field officers before the complaint is processed by the board itself.
We propose, further, that the Canada Labour Relations Board be reconstituted as a full-time body. Its members would no longer be representative of employees and employers. This provision has been somewhat misunderstood. We are not saying that members shall not have had a labour or management background. We are merely saying that once appointed to the board they must sever their connection with the organization or firm of employers, as the case may be, that they formerly represented or of which they were a member. There will, of course, be consultation with employers and the labour movement with respect to appointments. The Canada Labour Relations Board would have jurisdiction over unfair practices, deal with problems of successor rights, technological change, declarations of unlawful strikes and orders granting access to premises.
The predecessor bill proposed to clarify the law of picketing. The revised bill before the House has not carried forward that provision because of the representations received from both labour and management. Employers largely held the view that it extended the right to picket. Unions, on the other hand, were of the opinion that it infringed upon well established rights in Canada, rights that have been clearly supported in recent jurisprudence.
During the lifetime of a collective agreement, grievances are resolved by an arbitration process. The bill proposes to strengthen and better define the role of an arbitrator because we believe that arbitration is the only effective mechanism for the settlement of grievances. We have attempted to protect arbitrators' decisions from excessive judicial review.
I come now to the dispute settlement area which is perhaps one of the most important areas in the day to day administration of the legislation. The Minister of Labour is to be given increased flexibility in the use of techniques to attempt to bring about settlements. The minister would have the choice of taking no action at all or of appointing a conciliation officer, a one-man conciliation commission or a conciliation board. Should a conciliation officer be appointed and should he be unable to effect a settlement, the minister would be authorized to take no further action or to appoint a conciliation commission or a conciliation board.
Thus, depending on the circumstances prevailing, the minister would be free to use the appropriate agency to assist in resolving a dispute without being required to follow the present, more rigid procedure. May I say that the right to strike or lockout would arise seven days after the minister states his intention to take no further action or after the report of a conciliation commissioner or board has been received.
In addition to the use of conciliation procedures the minister may at any time appoint a mediator to assist the parties, but the intervention of a mediator would not in any way affect the timing of a strike or lockout. Provision has been made in the bill that in the event that a serious strike or lockout is threatened at a time when Parliament has been dissolved for an election, the governor in council may postpone until after the election the date on which the work stoppage would normally become legal. This power would be available only when the stoppage would adversely affect the national interest. The Minister of Labour would be required to report to Parliament at the earliest opportunity after the election.
I have left to the last the provisions of the bill dealing with technological change. As hon. members are aware, provisions regarding technological change were incorporated in the bill presented to this House by my predecessor on June 28, 1971. These provisions have been recast for the purpose of clarification, but before I discuss them I wish to express the philosophy of the government underlying these provisions.
Rapid change has become a fact of everyday life and we must recognize it as such. This government's position is clear, that it must encourage technological change if Canadians are to compete successfully in the years ahead in the world's rapidly changing economic environment. On the other hand, the government recognizes that technological change often seriously dislocates or adversely affects those employees directly involved and that such effects ought to be minimized.
Thus, we are faced with two seemingly conflicting goals: on the one hand the encouragement of technological change and, on the other, the desirability of minimizing adverse effects on employees. In studying the options, I believe that the best solution is found in the provisions of the bill. What we are seeking in these provisions is to encourage management and labour to deal with the impact of technological change on employees at the bargaining table. Industrial precedent proves that by working co-operatively labour and management can introduce major technological changes harmoniously.
Perhaps the greatest concern expressed by management about the technological change provisions is the possibility of the collective agreement being reopened during its term. The technological change provisions have been clarified to establish clearly that the collective agreement cannot be reopened where the employer gives notice of the intended technological change before the agreement was entered into, where the agreement establishes procedures by which the effects of the change may be negotiated and settled, or where there are substantive provisions contained in the agreement that the parties specify are intended to assist the employees affected by the change. Under these circumstances the collective
(Mr. O'Connell.]
March 29, 1972

agreement cannot be reopened. The technological change provisions would not apply to existing collective agreements but only to those made after the bill comes into force.
I might point out that the technological change provisions of the act require that before an application be granted by the Canada Labour Relations Board to reopen the contract, the board must be satisfied that a significant number of employees would be substantially and adversely affected. In the event that the Canada Labour Relations Board grants leave to negotiate, the bargaining would be limited to provisions that would assist employees affected by the change; there would be no bargaining over the change itself.
I would also like to outline very briefly the commitment my colleagues and I have made that the legislation needs to be supplemented in a determined and imaginative way by a number of non-legislative initiatives to reduce the undue emphasis on the adversary elements in employer-employee relationships. Among other initiatives, we will be reinforcing the industry specialist and mediation program. We will give new emphasis to labour-management consultation and conference activity and devise means to promote improved efforts by employers and trade unions in the field of industrial relations training. Our research effort will be strengthened.
I conclude by saying, Mr. Speaker, that I believe this proposed legislation is a step forward in the development of a sound legal framework for the process of free collective bargaining in the federal jurisdiction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-183, formerly Bill C-253, is an attempt to update the industrial relations section found in part V of the Canada Labour Code. One is impressed with the forceful arguments for change, if only through time, considering that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act has been unchanged since 1948. Consultations over the years with those affected by its provisions, and consultations with the provinces have indicated a need for change.
The Woods task force of 1968 in its intensive study also emphasized the need for amendments which would bring about a more meaningful piece of legislation. The public, too, especially of late, has registered its concern about the future of labour-management relations. The trend as presently seen points to more strikes, to the public interest being adversely affected, to loss of dollars, to questionable motives in bargaining, to lack of stability in labour-management relations, to additions to the unemployment rolls and to the deterioration of our competitive position.
It seems to me that labour-management relations are suffering from a sickness which calls for an immediate cure. They are in a deplorable state. In bargaining, it is obvious that confrontation, with emphasis on the adversary system, far outweighs the principle of bargaining in good faith. We are today attempting to inject a serum which will cure this illness. The people of Canada are
Canada Labour Code
demanding no less, and they should expect no less. This is the challenge.
The conditions to which I have referred affect the high hopes that Canadians cherish for the future in terms of social and economic goals. At a time when our ability to reach these goals is being strained by policies of our neighbours to the south and elsewhere, we must make certain that the legal framework we finally approve as a means of dealing with labour-management relations does not in other ways strain our ability to make progress.
We cannot be unduly harsh in our attitudes regarding management or labour interests. We do not wish to inject a climate, through legislation, which would have a detrimental effect on the continuing quest for industrial peace and the stabilization of collective bargaining relationships. Two things are certain. First, business needs maximum freedom, in this age of rapid technological change, to inject new ideas and innovations thereby maintaining its competitive position and improving its efficiency. Second, the workers need protection or a reasonable guarantee that they will not be thrown out on the street when these changes mean loss of jobs.
What is involved in all this? The labour law before us applies to industries within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada. These include interprovincial or international rail, road and pipe line transportation, shipping and related services, air transportation, interprovincial or international communications, telephone, telegraph or cable, radio and television broadcasting, and banks. Regardless of the jurisdictional aspect, it is well recognized that the provinces may, and often do, adopt in whole or in part legislation which is implemented federally. Here is another reason for making a conscious and determined attempt to bring forth the right bill.
I am not unnerved or impressed by the government's determination to proceed to the second reading of this measure only two days after the bill received first reading. The government can hardly construct an image of expeditious and decisive reform in this or any other area, whatever may happen in the weeks and months ahead. The fact is that this legislative statement of the government's intentions with regard to the Canada Labour Code is long overdue.
I should like to refer to a few of the highlights of the legislation before us because careful scrutiny must be directed toward all these aspects. I have a great deal of respect for the minister. I know he will recognize that our interest in this subject is as great as his and that he will turn a receptive ear to the suggestions we offer. We shall be dealing, as does the legislation, with questions which include the extension of bargaining rights, the appointment of a full-time labour relations board, a new definition of unfair practices, easier certification of unions, dispute settlements through the minister, enforcement procedures following collective agreements, technological change during the term of a collective agreement and rules in connection with strike action and picketing.
I heard what the minister said about the appointment of a full-time labour relations board. I am pleased he was able to explain some of the uncertainties. I was interested, too, in the new definition of unfair practices and in what was said about the certification of unions. There seems to
1272

March 29, 1972
Canada Labour Code
be some contradiction implicit in the procedure for certification as compared with de-certification. All these questions, as well as others, will be looked into.
The clauses dealing with technological change during the term of a collective agreement are concerned with a matter which has caused frustration and misgiving not only in business circles but among many who will be indirectly affected. The minister has already explained his stand with respect to the picketing aspect of the bill.
The extensively researched proposals of the Woods task force were made public in December, 1968. We waited until June 28, 1971, for the government's legislative response and now, in March of 1972, we are debating on second reading an amended version of that response. Mr. Speaker, the range, the soundness and the originality of the bill before us today hardly justifies such a prolonged gestation period. In fact, it has not been good for the country. Bill C-253, which was introduced on June 28, 1971, was ill-advised and added to the unacceptably high degree of uncertainty which already existed in the business community. The fact that industry and business has been waiting for this amended bill for the last eight months has undoubtedly cost people their jobs. After studying the highlights I can see no reason why the bill itself, or at least a declaration of intent, could not have been made public months ago.
A government can be excused for taking eight months to reach certain decisions, but not the kind of decisions embodied in this bill. To agonize for eight months over the changes which appear in this measure is pathetic; it is another indication of awesome indecisiveness and bad government. This is not the time for the government to seek to undertake a pretentious effort to speed the present bill through the House. To do so would not serve the government's cause, nor would it serve industrial relations in Canada.
My party wants to see this mini reform debated and decided before the next election. If this does not happen, it is only the government which is to blame. Proper consideration of this bill will call for open and serious discussion at the committee stage. The government has a high responsibility to ensure that experts from the labour, management and academic fields have an opportunity to comment on the legislation and suggest improvements. It is questionable whether this will actually be done when the bill gets into committee. I would remind hon. members that Bill C-253 created a furore because we did not know whether the proposed amendments, particularly those concerning technological change, were soundly based.
I will say that the minister did allay many of the fears which existed. I want to know whether there will really be an opportunity to become involved in discussions with the people I have mentioned. I notice the minister is nodding his head. I am grateful for that attitude. This is important when we are trying to improve the structure of labour legislation which directly affects the community. I am pleased that the minister should agree.
The success of this task will not be known simply by debate in this chamber but, rather, by how the reform is received in the human arena of free collective bargaining.

Our party is prepared to give cautious approval to this bill at the present time in view of the great number of changes relating to the technological aspects of the legislation. I say cautious also in view of the new innovation in regard to strikes.
We want to know whether in fact labour and business are happy with the subsequent amendments that will be brought in. We say that free collective bargaining has been the main foundation of industrial relations in a free society, and this bill does provide improvements to the structure of collective bargaining. Although I should like to say a few words on this matter, may I simply say we accept the use of bargaining procedures in preparing and equipping both employees and firms to deal with technological change.
As I said earlier, if technological change is not faced up to and not made more humane, we will not have adequate or sustained development or as fulfilling and just a society as possible. In scope, this bill provides an acceptable basis for parliament to reform the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. However, let me emphasize that sometimes we get into a hang-up on second reading. Some members seem to think that because a bill has had second reading that is the end of it, that the bill has been agreed to in principle which means it cannot be further amended. I do not accept that argument. I contend we are constantly improving the principle of bills and I want to make it very clear to this House that our party will be making extensive and substantial suggestions in committee for improving these proposals. We will be open and responsive to any suggestions and comments made by those in the community who have an interest and a stake in industrial relations.
However, Mr. Speaker, we are disappointed by the timidity of the entire bill. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent on a task force to provide ideas for a comprehensive overhaul of our industrial relations legislation. A plethora of creative and sound proposals was made by the task force and by many others concerned with industrial relations. There has been ample time and willingness in this House calmly and rationally to undertake a really comprehensive reform. However, I submit that the government has shied away from its big opportunity and I say it has let the country down. This is most evident in the challenge to find some way more effectively to reduce the necessity for strikes and lockouts and more reliably to protect the public interest.
I am very pleased with one part of the bill that has been brought to our attention and I am amazed that this provision has not been heretofore included in the code. I refer to what would happen if the members of the House of Commons were away beating on doors in June and strikes were called. I understand there is a provision in the bill to give the Governor General, or the governor in council, whichever is the correct terminology, power to deal with the situation. I recall one of my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party saying that when one of the members of my party wanted to inquire what would happen in such circumstances he was resorting to Nazi tactics, the tactics of fascism, I was quite surprised to hear that.

It has also been noted that after the technicians' strike it was also questioned whether the strike was a proper weapon. Perhaps we would have to go into the psychological reasons for strikes, whatever that may mean, but I shall not deal with that question now.
In our increasingly fragile and interdependent society, certain strikes and lockouts cannot be endured and must be disallowed. It is nonsense to suggest that they are always the only course of action. Parliament has intervened to protect the public interest when strikes in essential services have become unacceptably harmful. When the public interest is or has been adversely affected, then common sense is required and we should act in defence of the public interest. I subscribe to that contention, and so do some labour unions. Common sense has required such action in the past and will do so in the future. This subject is neither perverse nor academic, and the bill should have addressed itself to this area. I do not think it has, though it may have made an attempt. Perhaps when we get into committee the minister will explain why the procedure to which I have referred was not followed.
The Woods report dealt with this problem and made several proposals to improve the relationship of free collective bargaining and strikes and lockouts which have an intolerable and measurable effect on the public interest. This key suggestion was strongly endorsed at the annual meeting of our party and it should be in this bill. When parliament is not sitting, the minister has agreed that there is a procedure by which the Governor General can deal with the situation. We believe that when the public interest requires such action, it must remain the responsibility of parliament. Therefore, we feel that the recommendation of the Woods task force regarding a public interest disputes commission-I wonder where it went to-should have been developed legislatively. Such a body would be charged with determining special procedures for resolving industrial disputes in essential services. In addition, where strikes or lockouts occurred in essential areas this body would be responsible for advising parliament on how the public interest was being affected and on what action parliament might take.
This step would not roll back the right to strike or to lock out, nor would it end industrial conflict. However, it would provide parliament with a more comprehensive and informed basis on which to exercise the power it now has to legislate an end to a strike or lockout. Such a proposal is missing from the bill. I know the minister is charitable and I have a great deal of respect for him. I
Canada Labour Code
hope he will be able to convince his deputy that there is need for this sort of body charged with looking into the entire area of labour-management relations, thereby creating a climate that would eliminate the strike as a weapon because both sides are better informed.
Contrast this situation with the lack of information we are given by Treasury Board in regard to the Post Office Department. And who knows what is happening in the NABET negotiations? Ministers take the position that they feel it is not right to disclose matters that may affect negotiations while the negotiations are going on. We are about to go home for Easter and we cannot find out what is going on. Perhaps somebody knows. This sort of cat-and-mouse game, not only with labour-management but also with members, should not be permitted in an area of such vital concern. I think the establishment of an industrial disputes commission is a good idea and I see no reason why the government should not take action in this direction.
I want to deal with some of the amendments that the minister has brought in regarding technological change. He is quite right when he says that previously there was no opting out provision if notification was given of changes prior to the time of the signing of the contract. There was no reference to whether in fact the bill affected contracts in existence or which would come into existence at the time the bill was being debated. I think the minister has cleared up this matter, but there is still one point left. The right to strike is still there and we must look into this question.
As I said before, there is a feeling permeating the country, supported by labour, which I think is important, that perhaps we should look at another area. I will not deal with the amendments because I think the minister explained them well. The issue of technological change which creates such concern in terms of the amendments before us is of importance. We are hoping the committee's study will provide a basis acceptable to both labour and management-but we do not know that and this concerns me. I know labour was not happy with the 30-day notice they had to give. Whether this legislation has appeased labour, or whether business is prepared to go along with it remains to be seen. During the debate I think we have had co-operation. No one has bothered anyone, and I do not quite understand this. Perhaps because we know we are going home, and we have just been paid, has made everybody charitable.
The provision for collective bargaining during the length of a contract is not to be taken lightly. I emphasize this fact. Let me refer for a moment to this productive form of collective bargaining. Bill C-253 was certainly a mistake. The proposal of the former minister of labour would have weakened the efficacy of free collective bargaining in the interests of the workers of this country. My friends on my left, with their enthusiasm for that proposal, I would say are intellectually bankrupt. This bill places emphasis on dealing with the effects of technological change during the time a contract is renegotiated. It does not allow the reopening of a contract unless more sensible and available procedures are neglected. We can tighten up this provision. With his expertise, the minister perhaps
25104-22.!
