Canada Labour Code
can tighten it up sufficiently. In any event, we can explore this area.
This bill covers some 500,000 Canadian employees, many of whom are already negotiating contracts in respect of technological change. Even if this proposal provided such rights to unionized workers in both federal and provincial jurisdictions, which it does not, the two-thirds of the Canadian workers who are not unionized and are just as much affected by technological change would get nothing. We must admit that one-third of the working force is unionized while two-thirds are not. Even if every Canadian worker was unionized and reached by this reform, free collective bargaining could not do a complete job.
This is the main point we make this afternoon. As the Woods report pointed out, and as my party has, the achieving of a more humane and secure community in these times of rapid technological change requires the effective involvement of government in a whole range of economic and social areas. In meeting that challenge it seems to us this government has failed miserably and has made the situation worse. I will not get into that matter again during the debate this afternoon. Everybody knows what we on this side think of the government, but we will stick with this bill and see what happens.
The best climate for technological change for the worker is when there is growth of economic opportunity. Under this government we have had to endure restrictive, timid economic policies, a slowing down of assistance to research and development and no contemporary industrial strategy. Hopefully, this will change in the future under this government or the one that will be formed after June 27.
It is a fact that many of the effects and challenges of technological change to employees are primarily the responsibility of the federal government. Income maintenance, manpower mobility and retraining programs are essential instruments to help individuals deal with change. What is the government's record in this regard? Unemployment insurance reform which does not provide cost of living escalators will soon be inadequate. There have been no reforms or amendments to manpower mobility programs. We have seen a token in-industry retraining programs designed primarily to pad unemployment figures. There have been no changes to the manpower training program which has proven to be inadequate and inaccessible to those most poorly equipped to participate in our fast changing economy.
This bill will receive approval in principle because of the many good things it contains for the Canadian people. But, as I have said, we reserve the right to bring forward serious and substantial suggestions and amendments to improve the bill. In conclusion, I would like to state that the Toronto Star of yesterday reported in accurate terms what this whole thing is all about. I know hon. members have read the article, because we read everything we can get in this place, particularly when there is talk about labour-management relations. The last paragraph of this article reads:
The important thing to remember is that the interests of employer and worker may be in conflict in the short-term, but never in the long. Unless the employer can adapt to change and keep his

plant competitive, there will be no jobs. But if the employer does not manage change so as to cushion the impact on his work force, he will have bad labour relations whatever the law says.
We must arrive at an acceptable balance between the interests of business and labour. Hopefully, we will be able to arrive at the necessary solution in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members on this side of the House listened as attentively to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) as they did to the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) when he was explaining the provisions of this bill. It is difficult to criticize the hon. member for Hamilton West on his presentation, but he leaves me a little confused as to the stand his party takes on the legislation. This suggests to me the plight of people who become bowlegged from riding fences.
The hon. member suggested that we must maximize business freedom, but at the same time we must give the workers protection. I am wondering whether business needs maximum freedom and workers need only protection and a reasonable guarantee. What is wrong with workers having maximum freedom in dealing with environmental and social conditions? The hon. member, when speaking of the rights of labour, talked about the right to strike but then suggested that we must tighten things up. I ask him, through you, Mr. Speaker, what he was referring to when he said we must tighten things up. First he wants maximum freedom for the business community, and then he suggests we tighten things up in so far as collective agreements are concerned.
I believe the hon. member was being very considerate to one type of individual, but I do not think he would support any legislation which would weaken labour. I do not think his party would bring in the type of legislation, if perchance they had the opportunity to form the government, that would do harm to the Canadian worker. However, I am not certain I would want to give his party that opportunity. Only time will answer that question.
The legislation before us, Bill C-183 to amend the Canada Labour Code, the industrial relations process, is of the utmost concern to all organized workers, management and to most of the unorganized or John Doe people, the public of this country. All too often the non-organized and underpaid millions make no headlines. These people are so easily overlooked. Many people seem to doubt their existence in our society. This is why I believe it is necessary to bring in legislation that will put everybody on an equal footing so that the people of Canada may realize that those who are unorganized should have a say in so far as protection is concerned.
One might ask what this has to do with the bill now before us. I suggest the Canadian public wants legislation that would allow both management and labour to face modern-day, fast moving changes on an equal footing. I do not subscribe to one side having any advantage in this regard. Job security is the most important concern of the working man. The need to control mass lay-offs brought about by technological change is always uppermost in the minds of Canadians because whenever there is a technological change there are lay-offs which affect the purse
March 29, 1972

strings of the community. The community concerned must accept the situation.
Unless common sense, honesty and decency are practiced by employer and employee, there is room for concern. There must be a restoration of dignity in the job because this brings profit to industry, workers and the general public. Suspicion and hostility have cost the country dearly and this can be reversed only by a feeling of enthusiasm, understanding and co-operation. This bill in a small way does provide that type of relief from the never ending fear of employees that their jobs will be phased out without warning or consideration.
This legislation should also relieve the high tension of the employer in attempting to bring about technological change in the closed period of a contract. At least to some degree advance notice will have to be provided. Management must abandon the idea that the worker is bound to do what he is told simply because obedience is right, desirable or necessary. Every worker must be given the right to plan for change and must be told how change will affect him and his fellow workers.
The real purpose behind good industrial relations must be understanding and moderation. I believe the minister has understanding and I believe he will use moderation in the type of regulations which may be introduced with regard to this bill. If a worker is faced with new machines, new methods and organization which follow one another in rapid succession, if he is confronted with further changes before adaptation is completed, his tensions are multiplied and his fears become greater. If in fact he is told, without consultation with himself or his union, that his job is being sacrificed in the interest of alleged progress, his alarm and resentment will burst out in hostility. I suggest this is the reason we have had wildcat strikes and dissension throughout the country.
This is the type of consultation which should be carried on in respect of good industrial democracy as between management and labour. I hope the bill will provide some stability in this direction. I hope both management and labour can successfully work out industrial peace and contracts where little legislation is required. After all, legislation must be enforced, and this means third party intervention which should be required only in exceptional cases. It is not necessary to have the intervention of a third party if there is good will by the two parties concerned.
We in the New Democratic Party subscribe to the preamble of Bill C-183. While it may not add to the effectiveness of the bill, it does set out the desired goals for free collective bargaining in a democratic society. Sometimes I wonder if the Treasury Board negotiators and, indeed, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) have ever read, studied or employed good relations and constructive bargaining practices. One has only to read a reply to a question asked of the President of the Treasury Board to realize how shallow a government department is in so far as good industrial relations are concerned. I refer to issue No. 1 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the miscellaneous estimates committee. The President of the Treasury Board was asked a question in committee and his reply was as follows:
-I can assure you that strikes are not the kind of thing that the
Canada Labour Code
employer, particularly the federal government, encourages or tries to precipitate-
A member of the official opposition then asked:
Does this pose problems in a negotiating way to the federal government as the one employer with a very large bank roll?
The response to this question is what I am getting at in order to show that there are no meaningful negotiations by the Treasury Board in an attempt to bring about a solution to labour strikes. The response was:
In so far as the employee group-and this is one expectation they may have with a private company-hopes to bankrupt, if need be, the employer, the public service employees I do not think should nourish this particular hope. This is one significant difference.
A philosophy based on a test of economic strength obviously is not appropriate and should not be satisfactory to the public service employee. I think a number of them are recognizing this.
I suggest that with this type of approach to industrial relations it is no wonder we are in a mess in respect of the various contracts being negotiated by that department. As one goes through the bill, various words are used which need clarification if a battle as to legal interpretation is to be stopped before it begins. I am sure that those of us who are involved in looking at words in official contracts realize that the lawyers in this country have made millions of dollars because of the difficulty involved in interpreting sometimes just a small word.
Sometimes I think we would be better off if we used professors of English to write contracts rather than the legal people who normally write them. One word can make a great difference in the interpretation of a clause in a collective agreement. If we look at the interpretation placed on the word "strike", we see where work to rule could be considered to come under the interpretation. Sometimes work to rule or a slowdown can be, and has been, substituted for a strike. I am sure the minister is aware that this is so.
Many observations and representations have been made on the composition of the Canada Labour Relations Board. I was pleased to hear the minister say there will be consultation with employees and employers before people are appointed to the board. We will take him at his word, but we must be concerned about how another minister might do it. There may be merit in establishing a full-time Canadian Labour Relations Board with broadly increased powers and duties. However, nowhere does the bill spell out that members of the board will be equally representative of employees and employers-and one questions giving the governor in council such far reaching authority.
It is necessary to establish a board which fully represents management, labour and the public. All too often boards of this type are composed of learned friends without practical experience in the field for which they are given responsibility. It is absolutely necessary that this board not be composed of politicians, friends of the government, pork-barrel type of appointments, if we are really interested in bringing about sound, respected decisions affecting labour and management relations.

March 29, 1972
Canada Labour Code
I believe that the Minister of Labour will ensure proper representation on the board. We have heard his commitment with regard to the Canada Labour Relations Board. However, the minister and this government may not be here tomorrow or the day after and a new government may have an anti-union philosophy and fill the board with right-wing reactionaries. We should all be concerned about this. That is why we should have a form of guarantee that the Canada Labour Relations Board will be equally representative of the public, labour and management.
I believe that no provision should be embodied in the legislation which would permit anyone beyond the age of 65 to hold office on the board. This is my personal opinion. I see that there is a provision under which office can be held by a person up to the age of 70. The minister is aware of the many appointments being made of people close to retirement age and all too often an important body becomes strictly a hobby-horse for the people concerned. However, we agree that there are many exceptions in this regard. At the same time, if we had sound rules and sound legislation in so far as the age provision is concerned, I am sure it would be to the advantage of all concerned.
I believe, also, that the legislation should specify that women be represented on the board. I say this specifically for the hon. lady member of our party. Many male chauvinists see women only in a motherhood role, but the majority of the female species have much more than that to contribute. The fact remains that if there is to be a full-time board there must be effective communication between the minister and parties involved, otherwise the whole area of good industrial relations will fall down before the legislation gets off the ground.
In all seriousness I suggest that a woman should be appointed to the board. I think this would be a recognition of the views of the general public. My friends are suggesting just one woman, but I would not hesitate to say that there could be more than one.

This suggestion should be given consideration because all too often male chauvinists are appointed to boards and they are the people who end up on top. I am certain all members of the House recognize the importance of freedom of choice in deciding membership for various jurisdictions. Therefore it is important that we recognize the right of unions to apply for certification, and even more so, the importance of making a decision on the matter at the earliest possible time. In the past there have been lengthy delays in granting a vote to unions applying for certification.
A typical example is a union which applied for certification in April of 1971 in the Saskatoon area. On March 13, 1972, they received an acknowledgement that the situation was being considered. In the meantime the turnover in the plant had been tremendous, three of the key members were fired, which cut back on the certification application. Because of the passage of time and withdrawals from the company, the certification which they attempted to obtain no longer merited consideration by the board.
I hope that in spite of the amount of work the Canada Labour Relations Board will have, they will not become

bogged down in such situations because this can only result in the stirring up of hostilities. With hostility there is bound to be suspicion and work stoppage.
I should now like to speak about one of the most important concerns of the average worker whether he be in the retail business, in transportation, in industry, in the service industry or in any other industry. I refer to the provisions regarding technological change which are in the bill. It is becoming increasingly apparent that workers in all sections of our economy want some assurance with regard to job security. They are concerned, and rightly so, about technological changes which will make them obsolete or which will allow an insensitive management to charge them with being featherbedders.
Workers have a right in our democracy to expect humane treatment and consideration for the years of service they have contributed to industry. At the same time, surely no one disagrees that management has the right to expect a fair return on their investment. But this cannot be construed to mean that an employee can be turned loose without consideration being given to the contribution which he made to the success of that industry.
That is why the technological change provision in Bill C-183 is so important. That is why I consider that a loophole exists in the bill which may create unnecessary labour disputes between now and the time when many contracts will be open for negotiation. All contracts, whether open or closed, should be treated in the same way in so far as the technological provision in the bill is concerned. When enacted, this legislation should apply in exactly the same way to both open and closed contracts.
It may be expected that a number of industries will try to beat the gun by bringing about changes in their operation under the guise of introducing new operations, although I hope I am proven wrong. Such could be the interpretation of the wording in the legislation where reference is made to a change that is directly related to the introduction of equipment or material. I believe that a change is a change, and whether or not it is directly related to the introduction of equipment or material will not soften the impact.
I should also point out that concern is expressed because no coverage is provided for the shutdown or transfer of a railway terminal. Perhaps this matter is covered in collective agreements. I believe that is the case with most of them. But one has only to refer to the words of Mr. Justice Samuel Freedman to realize the seriousness of the matter. What he said is very important. The minister referred in committee to what Mr. Justice Freedman said. I should like to quote a chapter from the report by Mr. Justice Freedman on technological change-an economic and human problem. He quotes Dr. John T. Deutsch, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada. The quotation reads as follows:
We are confronted with the problem of how to deal with displacement and dislocation, with the need for retraining, with the development of new skills, with the survival of an enterprise and the investment of new capital, with material and human losses, and with the question of how to distribute new benefits between wages, social welfare and leisure. These are complex and rapidly changing issues which cannot be tackled successfully unless; first, there is mutual concern and mutual recognition of the legitimate role of each party; second, there is realization that neither the
March 29, 1972

responsibility for nor the cost of adjustment can be imposed solely upon one of the parties or let fall upon the weak; and third, there is a comprehension of the need for objective analysis, for information, for prior study, for consultation and forward planning, and for a readiness to deal with realities,
Mr. Freedman quoted Dr. Deutsch and there is much wisdom in the words quoted. Mr. Freedman wrote:
There is much wisdom in the words above quoted, and the commission is pleased to adopt them as the basis of its approach to the problem now being considered. So well do they define that problem and expose its implications that an extended treatment of it by the commission is hardly necessary.
In the same vein, Mr. Speaker, he quotes Messrs. Somers, Cushman and Weinberg's "Adjusting to Technological Change" as follows:
This differentiation between beneficiaries and sufferers from technological change presents us with a moral as well as an economic problem. Society as a whole is, by and large, a beneficiary. Is it morally acceptable for most of us to enjoy the benefits of new technologies without utilizing every possible means of minimizing the losses and assisting the readjustment of those who are not beneficiaries but sufferers? Society has a moral obligation to accept the cost of necessary programs to this end as a charge against the benefits of technological advance.
In that regard, Mr. Speaker, I suggest we should realize that whether the contract is open or closed, or whether it has another three years to run, there should not be any technological change that would bring suffering to the workers.

I assure the minister that the New Democratic Party will be pressing for this change consistently, and until it is brought about debate will be protracted. We consider this to be one of the most important areas omitted from this bill, and of course we will be watching it.
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party will be watching a number of other areas very closely. We question why a change was made from the previous act in that "approximate" is now used in referring to notice being served concerning technological change. Why would the positive approach as to how many employees are likely to be affected be replaced by the word "approximate", which leaves room for argument and interpretation and long and costly legal battles? Why is a word such as "significant" used, which again leaves a veil of doubt and suspicion, and a word like "substantially" when talking about an order to serve notice to bargain? Why the change from the first to the seventh day when talking about the right to strike or lockout being limited during the period between parliaments?
These and other questions will be asked when this bill goes to committee and we have an opportunity to question the minister and hear briefs from interested parties. Even with reservations, we in this party intend to vote for this bill on second reading. When that is completed it will go to committee and there we will ask the type of question that is in the minds of many, in order to find out precisely whether industrial relations are adequately covered in this bill.
We all want equality and a healthy nation. However, no one relishes compulsion because compulsion in one area
Canada Labour Code
can only lead to more compulsion. When some hon. members talk about how we will bring about compulsion in regard to labour, we question where this leads. The answer is that it will lead to more compulsion in other areas. This is not what Canadians desire; rather, they desire good labour management relationships bringing peace and stability through true, uninhibited collective bargaining.
Mr. Speaker, we wish the minister well with this bill. We hope that at some time he or one of his colleagues will stand in this House and state that some of the thoughts we have expressed will be given favourable consideration. All employees are entitled to this.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is normal to make a few remarks at this stage of the proceedings on Bill C-183, entitled "An Act to amend the Canadian Labour Code". I wish to point out that I took some time to peruse the preamble of the bill. It is very interesting to note the good intentions showing through the purported principles of this bill.
Unfortunately, we see that the purpose aimed at is not always achieved, since the tensions that exist in labour-management relations are certainly no indication that those relations are good and that the methods of settling disputes are effective.
The recommendations contain provisions for the remuneration of the members of the Canada Labour Relations Board, the establishment of offices where it is deemed necessary, the remuneration and expenses of members of the Board in relation to matters investigated and, lastly, the setting up of the whole bureaucracy deemed necessary for the implementation of the various provisions of the act.
I can very well understand that it is not always easy to maintain a constant balance between the fair claims of labour and the requirements of the common good. However, labour legislation must aim at such an objective.
Bill C-183 contains a few amendments as to the administration of the law, in cases of technological changes. It varies somewhat from the present legislation in that its clauses relating to technological changes will not affect collective agreements already in effect, but they will apply after the adoption of this bill. From now on, any employer who is bound by a collective agreement and who intends to effect a technological change must advise the union in writing 90 days prior to the proposed change and he must indicate: (a) the nature of the change; (b) the approximate number of employees who will be so affected and (d) the effect of the changes on employment security.
Should the employer not comply with these requirements, the union is empowered to appeal to the Canada Labour Relations Board and request action. The Board will order the employer to suspend the application of the clauses relating to technological changes for a period of 90 days. Upon a request by a union, the Board will also be empowered to order the employer to negotiate new labour conditions if the changes affect clearly and unfavourably the terms and conditions or security of employment.

March 29, 1972
Canada Labour Code
What happens in the case of failure to negotiate? Will the unions be able to strike? The new bill does not throw any light on this point.
In fact, it would appear from clause 180 dealing with the right to strike, that the union involved in technological changes allowing for a re-examination of the collective agreement will be in a position to strike provided all the requirements set forth in clause 180 are met. One exception deals with a strike during an election campaign when it goes against the national interests. The governor in council can then prohibit such a strike by order in council until 7 days after the elections have taken place.
There has been also a new amendment to insure that an employee must pay his union funds, at the source or directly, when it is so stipulated in the collective agreement. This is a very strange concept of union freedom. I would now like to point out that in my opinion, real freedom for unions should be clearly established by taking into consideration two points in particular: the freedom to join the union, or to get out of it. This is real freedom for unions.
This bill also proposes to continue the Canada Labour Relations Board in order to make it, as had been suggested by the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey), a full-time body made up of a chairman, a vice-chairman and four members. If necessary, another vice-chairman and four other members at the most could be added.
Under present circumstances, I think we should rather set up a board of experts secure from undue influences, a group experienced people familiar with labour and management problems; a few experts who could provide accurate data on variations in the cost of living and determine basic wages for workers in various types of industries or services, taking into account all the necessary factors to ensure normal production of goods or services.
There is such a thing as a labour board made up of competent men! What we have to do is assure them of a fair salary and give them the power to make decisions.
In public services, the economic power resulting from the right to strike could be replaced by some adequate mechanism for salary adjustments based on the cost of living index. Let us stop thinking in terms of compulsory contributions or arbitration and start considering a fair and equitable distribution of corporation profits and of workers' salaries, and we will have peaceful labour-management relations. The solution will not be arrived at without effort, but the present situation makes it mandatory that we take appropriate steps if we truly want to avoid anarchy.
Responsible workers, a high percentage of whom have families to support, are entitled to demand some degree of happiness for their dependents, but they should be able to do so without being forced to resort to strikes, when they can unwittingly be the instrument of an enemy using them to promote subversive interests.
Strikes merely lead the worker into a vicious circle. He might get a little more, but will he be better off, after the effects of the strike have ceased and new taxes bring down the value of money and make him consider another strike?
I have here an editorial of Station CJRC on strikes. I quote:
Strikes are in style. They have become so frequent that they are no longer being kept count of.
We shall be asked to keep calm, told that the rights of workers are sacred and that the strikes of others always seem more reprehensible. But facing that rising tide of walk-outs, all equally costly, let us ask whether such folly will not lead us straight to disaster.
Here is a typical example of a stupid strike: the air controllers. Basically, their 11-day strike gained them a 7 per cent increase in salary. Arbitration, it will be remembered, suggested 15.8 per cent over a period of 27 months. They were offered 17 per cent a few days later. Confrontation led to another arbitration decision, granting them 16.5 per cent. To obtain a 7 per cent salary increase, the controllers lost 11 days' pay-they have no strike fund-causing a loss to the air companies of $22 million, not to speak of inconvenience and expense caused to passengers, who had to bear them with patience and selflessness. Was it worthwhile?
Those in favour of strikes could perhaps benefit by such soulsearching. This might avoid the catastrophe which seems imminent. It is not a matter of being pessimistic, but of being realistic. It is high time.
Before deeper involvement in strikes, workers should give it serious thought. They do have rights which must receive recognition, but there are also rights, and responsibilities related to young people to whom other alternatives than strikes should be taught.
Unions remain democratic instruments of protection for workers, provided they are directed by leaders aware of their responsibilities to their members and the means resorted to in order that management recognize its social responsibilities.
In view of the trend towards centralization, one is often inclined to forget the adequacy of human communication required in order to understand employees' grievances. Necessarily, an instrument of consultation must be established and maintained constantly on the alert, particularly as concerns changing working conditions. It is not normal to give up the morale and well-being of employees for the sake of efficiency, service or performance.
In a fluid situation, as a result of the rigidity of policies of the authorities in command, there grows among employees the desire to test the right to strike.
Labour laws should be formulated with clarity, thus allowing the average worker to grasp their meaning without having too often to consult lawyers, who do not seem to need to go on strike to increase their fees.
Let all those responsible for legislation get their inspiration from the same principles behind the salary adjustments put forward in the case of ministers, hon. members, senators, judges and a group of senior officials, and we will then undoubtedly have laws which will be aimed at preventing useless and harmful strikes.
The right to live, for every individual, stems from a natural right. It must be recognized way before the right to strike or to make exaggerated profits, and the necessary steps must be taken by those who are responsible for legislation, to ensure first of all that each and every one has in fact the right to live. We should be clear-sighted enough to set up a system for the intelligent distribution of existing goods without having recourse to strikes, when the majority of the citizens want to work.

March 29, 1972

Hopefully, this bill will improve somewhat the situation in a field where solutions are imperative.
